vignette:
He is 42, an electrician who has spent most of his adult life in other people's ceilings, under houses, and on ladders, tracing faults with steady hands. Before the assault, he thinks of himself as someone practical and even-tempered. He works hard, comes home tired, cooks on weekends with his partner, and likes the predictability of tools laid out where they belong. He is not a man who talks much about feelings, but he has always believed he can handle himself.

The assault happens on an ordinary weeknight, which is part of what stays with him. He finishes a late job and stops at a small bottle shop on the way home. In the car park, a man he does not know asks for money. He says no and keeps walking. He remembers the scrape of shoes behind him, then a voice close to his ear, sharp and aggressive. By the time he turns, the first blow has already landed. He falls awkwardly against the side of his ute. He can still recall the metallic thud, the smell of stale alcohol on the man's breath, and the shock of realizing this is really happening. There are more hits than he can count clearly. He tries to shield his head. He hears himself making a strange sound, half-grunt, half-plea. What he remembers most is not pain at first but helplessness-the sudden certainty that he has no control over whether this stranger stops.

Someone from the shop comes out and shouts. The attacker runs. In the aftermath there are fluorescent lights, police questions, a hospital curtain, his partner's face gone pale with fear. He tells everyone he is lucky. No broken bones, only bruising, stitches near his eyebrow, a cracked rib. He says the words as if that should settle it. For the first week he mostly feels numb and embarrassed. He hates that people at work see his swollen face. He shrugs off their concern, jokes that he should have ducked faster.

Then the nights begin to change. He starts waking abruptly, heart hammering, drenched in sweat, already braced for another blow. Sometimes he dreams the attack exactly as it happened; sometimes in the dream the attacker is faceless, or his partner is the one being cornered and he cannot move. He begins checking the locks two or three times before bed. If a car door slams outside, his whole body jolts. He sleeps on the side of the bed closest to the hallway, telling himself he is just being careful.

At work, the changes are harder to hide. He has always relied on concentration, especially when working live boards or troubleshooting in cramped spaces. Now he finds himself drifting. A sudden noise on a construction site-a dropped length of conduit, raised voices between contractors-sends a surge through him so fast that he steps back before he can think. He starts scanning every place he enters, noting exits, who is standing where, who seems agitated. In customers' homes he is polite but tense, especially if a man comes too close behind him while he is bent over a switchboard. Once, when a client's teenage son appears unexpectedly in the garage, he whirls around with such force that he bangs his elbow and drops his screwdriver. He laughs it off, but afterward he sits in the ute for ten minutes, shaking.

His partner notices that his world is getting smaller. He no longer stops at shops after dark. He avoids the bottle shop entirely and takes a longer route home to bypass that street. Friends invite them to a pub, and he makes excuses. Crowds feel dangerous; even standing in line for coffee makes his chest tighten. He becomes irritable over minor things-traffic, noise, a misplaced charger-then goes quiet with shame. He knows his partner is trying to be gentle when she asks if he is okay, but sometimes even that feels unbearable, as if she is standing too close to something raw. He says, "I'm fine," more sharply than he means to.

What troubles him most is the sense that the assault is still happening in pieces. He can be driving to a job at dawn and suddenly see, with full clarity, the attacker's shoulder lunging toward him. His hands clamp on the steering wheel. His jaw aches from clenching. He has begun to feel wary of strangers in a way that does not fit the man he used to be. He does not like this version of himself-suspicious, restless, easily startled-but he cannot seem to switch it off.

Months later, the bruise around his eye is long gone, and the scar at his eyebrow has faded into a pale line. People assume he is back to normal. He goes to work, pays bills, answers messages, and keeps moving. But his days are organized around avoiding reminders and managing the constant sense of threat. By evening he is exhausted from holding himself together. Lying in bed beside his partner, listening for noises outside, he tells himself he should be over it by now. Instead he stays awake in the dark, waiting for his body to believe he is safe.
